name: Lumbar support cushion / seat wedge

lead: A lumbar cushion fills the gap between your lower back and the chair, and a seat wedge tilts the pelvis forward. While in use, they put you in a more upright seated position with the lower-back curve supported.

The cushion supports the lumbar curve and the wedge changes the pelvic angle. Published research is small: a 2000 study looked at back muscle activity with and without a cushion, and a small military-aviation study looked at pilots with low back pain. Neither measured appearance.

paras: People place the cushion or wedge on an office chair, car seat or couch and use it through the workday, usually alongside regular movement breaks and posture exercises.
No adverse effects are documented in the sources consulted. Some people find the position uncomfortable at first, and persistent back pain is a reason to see a clinician.

angle.text: Lumbar cushions and seat wedges prop the lower back and tilt the pelvis so you sit more upright while using them. Small studies have looked at back muscle activity and back pain.

lead: A lumbar support cushion is a pad placed between the lower back and a chair backrest to support the inward curve of the lumbar spine, and a seat wedge is a tapered cushion that tilts the pelvis forward when sitting. People use them to sit more upright, which gives a taller, straighter seated posture and a less slouched upper body and head position when working at a desk or driving.[1][2]

The idea draws on how the pelvis and lower back set the posture of everything above them. The lumbar spine normally curves inward, and a forward or backward tilt of the pelvis changes that curve.[3] Support at the lower back is meant to keep the pelvis in a neutral position and reduce the rounding that tends to appear in long sitting sessions. A detachable lumbar cushion in a backpack study increased pelvic tilt angle and reduced sternocleidomastoid tone, without significantly changing forward trunk lean or craniovertebral angle.[4]

Research on the products themselves is small and focuses on comfort and function: a pilot study of lumbar cushions, a study of forward-inclining wedges in workers with limited hip flexion and a study of lateral wedges in adolescent scoliosis.[5][2][1] No trial has tested them for appearance outcomes.
infobox: Lumbar curve, pelvic tilt, seated posture

paras: Patent records show lumbar cushions in contoured, adjustable and portable inflatable forms, including a 1989 US patent for a rotationally contoured cushion and several inflatable designs filed from 2002 onward.[6][7] Seat wedges are tapered foam cushions that raise the back of the seat to tilt the pelvis forward, and some designs are angled to one side for use with a curved spine.[2][8]

The lumbar spine has a natural inward curve, and its depth is related to pelvic tilt; a forward pelvic tilt exaggerates the arch while sitting for long periods is linked in the literature to muscle imbalances that change posture.[3] A pad behind the lower back fills the gap between spine and backrest. A forward-inclining wedge changes the angle at the hips and has been found to reduce the compensatory lumbar flexion of seated workers with limited hip flexion.[2]

Forum members mention sitting with a lumbar cushion along with other seating aids for comfort during long hours at work.[9] Users report relief and a more upright seat; the posture benefit is described in user accounts rather than in appearance studies.

A 2000 study from Serbia examined eight military helicopter pilots with low back pain during prolonged forced sitting. It compared sitting with and without a lumbar cushion on separate days, and six of eight had lower paraspinal muscle activity after using the cushion.[1]

A 2014 study of twelve seated workers with limited hip flexion found that lumbar flexion decreased significantly on a forward-inclining wedge compared with a level seat or a backward-reclining wedge.[2] A 2023 study of 99 adolescents with idiopathic scoliosis found the greatest correction of scoliosis angle with wedges raised on the same side as the curve's convexity.[5] A 2026 trial in 28 healthy men found a lumbar cushion in a backpack increased pelvic tilt angle and reduced sternocleidomastoid tone.[4] No studies found of seat wedges or lumbar cushions for posture appearance.
